name: Raw milk

lead: Raw milk is milk that has not been heat-treated. In looksmaxxing and primal-diet circles it is drunk for a nutrient-dense, enzyme-rich food that supporters say helps skin, hormones, digestion and, in adolescents, height.

Proponents say heat destroys enzymes, immunoglobulins, vitamins and beneficial bacteria, so unheated milk keeps more of them active. A 2011 systematic review of 40 studies found pasteurization lowers some vitamins (B1, B2, C, folate) slightly and has a minimal effect on overall nutritive value. Some forum members note that milk cannot change bone length after growth plates fuse.

paras: People buy it from farms or shops where sale is allowed and drink it as a staple, often as part of carnivore or primal eating, with some discussing large intakes for body-composition goals. Reports of results come from personal experience over weeks to months.

Raw milk can carry Listeria, Salmonella, E. coli and Campylobacter, and pregnant women, children, older adults and immunocompromised people are at greatest risk of serious illness. Public-health literature also links it to brucellosis and tick-borne encephalitis. Legal status varies: some places ban retail sale, others allow farm sales with labels. Some forum members report acne or bloating.

chain: Claimed growth, skin and digestion gains
angle.text: In primal and carnivore-style circles raw milk is drunk for height in adolescents, clearer skin, digestion and hormones, on the idea that unheated milk keeps more nutrients and enzymes active. A 2011 review found pasteurization changes nutritive value only minimally.

lead: Raw milk, also called unpasteurized milk, is milk from cows, goats, sheep or other animals that has not been heat-treated to reduce microbes. In appearance-focused communities it is discussed as part of 'primal' or carnivore-style eating, with claims about skin, digestion, hormones and, for adolescents, height.[1][2]

A 2011 systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 studies found that pasteurization lowered vitamins B1, B2, C and folate, raised or left others unchanged, and had minimal effect on the milk's overall nutritive value; it also found no sound evidence that raw milk prevents or treats allergies, cancer or lactose intolerance.[3] A small randomized pilot study on lactose intolerance did not find that raw milk was better tolerated than pasteurized milk.[4]

Public-health literature links raw milk to infections including listeriosis, brucellosis, salmonellosis and tick-borne encephalitis, and describes its microbiota as a mix of beneficial, spoilage and pathogenic organisms.[5][6][7][8] Rules differ widely by country and US state.[1]
infobox: Varies: banned for retail in several countries; some US states allow sales

paras: Raw milk is milk that has not been pasteurized, a heating process that reduces the number of viable pathogenic bacteria and extends shelf life.[1][3] Some traditional cheeses are made from raw milk, and fermented products such as kefir are made from milk with grains of yeasts and bacteria; these are separate products from drinking raw milk itself.[1][9]

Raw milk contains a complex community of microorganisms that enter from the udder, the environment and equipment. Reviews describe some as useful for dairy fermentation or associated with health (lactobacilli, bifidobacteria) and others as spoilage organisms or pathogens such as Listeria, Salmonella, E. coli and Campylobacter.[6]

Dairy animals were domesticated roughly 9000 to 7000 BC in Mesopotamia, and for most of history milk was consumed unheated.[1] Louis Pasteur developed pasteurization in 1864, and the process was introduced in the United States in the 1890s.[1]

According to Wikipedia, milk accounted for about a quarter of food and waterborne outbreaks in the US before World War II and now accounts for under 1%, which authors attribute largely to pasteurization.[1] Regulation followed in many places, for example the US ban on interstate sale for human consumption in 1987 and Canada's prohibition of direct sales in 1991.[1]

Advocacy groups describe raw milk as a more complete food, claiming that heat destroys vitamins and enzymes and that raw milk can help with allergies, cancer and lactose intolerance.[3] In looksmaxxing forums, posters echo this, adding claims about skin, hormones, gut health and, for young people, growth hormone and height.[10]
Other members argue the opposite: one thread contends that raw milk and raw-meat 'primal' diets cannot reshape facial bone structure once growth plates have fused, calling such hopes 'cope'.[11]

The 2011 meta-analysis reported decreases in some vitamins after pasteurization (B1, B2, C, folate), no significant effect on B6, and an increase in vitamin A, concluding that the effect on nutritive value was minimal.[3]

Studies in children raised on farms have associated raw milk with fewer allergies and asthma, but, as Wikipedia notes, the protective effect may reflect the farm environment in general rather than the milk.[1] A letter on a randomized trial asked whether yoghurt could be an acceptable alternative to raw milk for reducing infant eczema and allergy.[12]

Health agencies such as the US CDC record outbreaks linked to raw milk; Wikipedia cites 144 raw-milk-linked outbreaks in the US from 2007 to 2016.[1] Pasteurized milk is not risk-free: a 1983 Massachusetts listeriosis outbreak was traced to a brand of pasteurized milk.[13]

Infections associated with raw milk or raw dairy products include listeriosis (especially from soft raw-milk cheeses, with greatest danger to pregnant women, newborns and immunocompromised adults), brucellosis, tick-borne encephalitis, and Q fever.[5][7][8][14] A 2024 study found influenza A virus could survive in refrigerated raw milk during the US H5N1 dairy cattle outbreak.[1]
Forum posters themselves list bacterial risk from poor sources, acne and bloating among the downsides.[10]

Wikipedia summarizes regional rules: Canada has prohibited direct sales since 1991; US rules vary by state; Australia has banned drinking-milk sales since the 1940s; Brazil has banned sales since 1969; the UK permits farm and market sales with warning labels; in Europe rules differ by country.[1]

No studies found of raw milk for appearance, skin or height. Related human research includes a randomized pilot study of raw milk and lactose intolerance and a 2011 meta-analysis of pasteurization and vitamin content.[3][4]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, raw milk appears in threads about primal diets, height, skin and testosterone, with some users enthusiastic and others dismissive.[10][11]
